text.title: JTBD Switch Interview Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for running a Switch (Forces of Progress) interview and writing the 4-force artefact: who may be recruited, the backwards timeline, the question forms that are forbidden, and what each of push / pull / anxiety / habit must carry before it may be scored.

rule.statement: Interviewee MUST have completed a real purchase or switch, and the purchase date MUST be within 90 days of the interview (60 preferred). Prospects, trial users who never paid, and churned-long-ago users are excluded; `switch_decision` may not be set to `switched` without a purchase date in the transcript.
rule.rationale: The forces are reconstructed from episodic memory of one specific week. Past roughly three months the episodic detail decays into a rehearsed summary, and the interviewee supplies tidy reasons instead of the events that actually moved them.

rule.statement: The interview MUST start at the moment of purchase and walk backwards: Buying → Deciding → Active Looking → second triggering event → Passive Looking → First Thought. The artefact records a timestamp or datable anchor for each of those transitions.

rationale.source: Cognitive interview technique — reverse-order recall (Fisher & Geiselman)

rule.rationale: Forward chronology lets the subject narrate a story they have already told themselves. Reverse order breaks the rehearsed script and forces each step to be anchored to the adjacent known-true fact, which is why forensic interviewers use it to recover detail.

rule.statement: Questions MUST be about events and context — when, where, who else was in the room, what device, what did you do immediately after. "Why did you choose us", "what features do you want", and any hypothetical ("would you pay for…") are forbidden and must not appear in the transcript.

rationale.source: Nisbett & Wilson 1977, Telling More Than We Can Know

rule.rationale: People have no privileged access to the causes of their own choices and will fluently generate a plausible reason on demand. A why-question therefore returns a confabulation that is indistinguishable, in the transcript, from a real cause.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST name what was fired: the prior product, a manual workaround (spreadsheet, WhatsApp thread), a person (agency, assistant), or an explicit "nothing — the problem was tolerated". A blank or absent fired-alternative fails validation.

rationale.source: Christensen, Hall, Dillon & Duncan — Competing Against Luck (2016)

rule.rationale: A job is defined by what got hired in place of something else. Without the fired alternative you have a description of your own product, and the true competitive set — usually a workaround, not a vendor — never enters the analysis.

rule.statement: Each of push, pull, anxiety, habit MUST carry at least one verbatim quote in `verbatim_quotes` before it may be scored. A force the interview did not surface is written as `null`, never as `0`.

rationale.source: Forces of Progress four-force model (Moesta / Re-Wired Group)

rule.rationale: Anxiety and habit are almost never volunteered — the buyer does not narrate their own inertia. Scoring an unsurfaced force as zero converts a gap in the interview into a positive finding that the force was absent, and the resulting report tells the team to stop working on the one thing blocking the switch.

rule.statement: The report MUST state whether push + pull exceeded anxiety + habit for this interviewee, and name the single force that was decisive at the Deciding step.
rule.rationale: The reflex response to a stalled switch is to add pull — more features, a better demo, a discount. When the binding force is anxiety (risk of the new thing) or habit (sunk investment in the old), added pull moves nothing, because those two forces are addressed by guarantees, migration and onboarding, not by the product surface.

rule.statement: The First Thought and Active Looking transitions MUST each be tied to a datable event — a lost client, a price rise, a failed audit, a new hire, a device that died — not to a standing condition ("we were growing", "it was getting messy").
rule.rationale: Standing conditions persist for years without producing a purchase. The event is what converted a tolerated condition into active demand, and it is the only part of the timeline that a campaign or a trigger-based touch can actually target.
